pagetitle: "Where the back-ends differ"
---

# Where the back-ends differ

Three back-ends ship: LaTeX (and the PDF it typesets), HTML, and EPUB. The
marking syntax means the same thing in all of them. What the indexes can do
differs, because the tools underneath them do.

EPUB and HTML build the same index out of the same document nodes, so every
row below that says "in HTML" is true of EPUB too. The two places EPUB parts
company with HTML — a book is one Pandoc process there, and its locators are
sequence numbers with no pages behind them — are on the [EPUB](epub.qmd) page.

1. **No level ceiling in HTML.** Sub-entries nest as deep as you write them.
   The three-level ceiling described on [Sub-entry
   levels](sub-entry-levels.qmd) is `makeindex`'s limit, not the
   extension's.
2. **The one-entry warning is LaTeX-only.** A term marked two different ways
   reaches the LaTeX index tool as one entry the extension had to compose, so
   the extension says it did. An HTML index prints the locator and the
   cross-reference together on one entry by itself, with nothing to compose,
   so the warning would name a decision that format never has to make.
3. **Sorting is the extension's own in HTML.** Top-level entries are ranked
   into letter groups first; inside a group, and at every level below the top,
   the order folds ASCII uppercase to lowercase and then compares character
   codes, breaking a tie by character code, over an entry's sort key where it
   has one. In LaTeX the order is `makeindex`'s. Neither collates accented or
   non-Latin text the way a language would, which is what sort keys are for.
4. **Locators are numbered links in HTML**, in the order the marks are
   written, where LaTeX gives page numbers.
5. **Cross-reference targets are hyperlinked in HTML** when the target names an
   entry in the same index, and are plain text otherwise. A printed index
   cannot link at all.
6. **A cross-reference carries no locator in any back-end.** The `see also`
   limitation described on [Cross-references](cross-references.qmd) is the
   same in all of them.
7. **The principal mention is emphasized everywhere**, but by different means:
   the LaTeX back-end wraps the page number in a command you can redefine, and
   the HTML back-end marks the link with a class and a `<strong>`.
8. **A page range is a page range only in LaTeX.** `makeindex` prints one span
   of pages, `12--15`; HTML has no pages, so a range there is one numbered link
   at the opening mark. Both are one locator where you wrote two marks, which
   is what the syntax means.
9. **The extension's own words and marks are settable in HTML and EPUB.** The
   `Symbols` group heading, the `see` and `see also` in front of a
   cross-reference, and the punctuation inside an entry are the extension's
   rather than yours, and `index-labels:` — keys `symbols`, `see`, `see-also`,
   `separator` and `xref-separator`, written at a document's top level or
   inside one `indexes:` entry, the nearer setting winning key by key — sets
   them for the HTML and EPUB indexes. It reaches the LaTeX back-end nowhere:
   that one emits `\see` and `\seealso`, whose two words babel supplies from
   your document's `lang:`. There is no third word to set there — a LaTeX index
   has no letter groups at all, so it prints no `Symbols` heading for
   `symbols:` to override. Neither separator key reaches it either: what stands
   between a term and its page numbers there is `makeindex`'s own delimiter,
   and what stands between two cross-references is written into the LaTeX this
   extension emits — in two places, the command it defines for a term carrying
   both kinds and the join it writes when a term's targets ride the
   encapsulation channel instead.
10. **All three back-ends follow `lang:`, and share nothing else about it.**
    Every back-end picks its own words from your document's language, and
    that language is the whole of what they have in common: LaTeX asks babel,
    HTML and EPUB read a table this extension ships. Two consequences follow.
    The languages covered are not the same — babel covers hundreds, this
    extension covers Spanish, French, German and Italian, and German only in
    part, so a document in a language babel knows and this table does not gets
    a localized PDF and an English HTML index. And `index-labels:` is read by
    the HTML and EPUB back-ends alone, so a word you set there changes those
    two indexes and never the PDF, where babel's word stands. Setting a word
    for both means writing `index-labels:` for HTML and EPUB and redefining
    `\seename` or `\alsoname` for LaTeX.
